canonical_statement: The study aimed to evaluate the clinical utility of the DCNN-based MC-100i digital morphology analyzer by comparing AI-assisted smear review with conventional manual microscopy in routine multicenter practice.
The study used a prospective, multicenter, randomized paired crossover method-comparison design in which the same smear was assessed by AI-assisted digital morphology and manual microscopy.
Eligible residual EDTA-anticoagulated blood samples met International Consensus Group 41-rule criteria for smear review or were submitted at a clinician request.

population.label: Residual EDTA-anticoagulated blood samples requiring smear review
inclusion_criteria: Met ICG 41-rule smear-review criteria or clinician-requested smear review

canonical_statement: Fresh residual whole-blood samples were collected from three Chinese tertiary hospitals between March 2023 and October 2023.

population.label: Patients represented by residual blood samples from three participating hospitals

canonical_statement: Four Center 2 smears were excluded because informed consent was not obtained, leaving 1,570 smears for the paired analyses.

population.label: Analyzed peripheral blood smears
exclusion_criteria: Four Center 2 smears excluded because informed consent was not obtained

canonical_statement: The analyzed cohort comprised 656 smears from Center 1, 306 from Center 2, and 612 from Center 3.

population.label: Analyzed peripheral blood smears across three centers

canonical_statement: Approximately 99.8% of enrolled samples required manual microscopy review under laboratory rules or clinical request.

population.label: Analyzed smears requiring manual microscopy review

canonical_statement: Three Wright-Giemsa-stained smears (A, B, and C) were prepared per sample with the same SC-120 automated smear stainer; smear A was used for both paired workflows and smears A-C supported the reference assessment.
Within each center, samples were randomized 1:1 to AI-first or manual-first reading sequences, with at least a two-week washout between readings.
The nucleated-cell module accepted 224 x 224 RGB cell images and used convolutional, pooling, residual, fully connected, and softmax components to output cell-class probabilities and labels.
The red-cell grading and platelet-estimation modules used an object-detection framework with 416 x 416 RGB images to localize and classify individual red cells and platelets.
For AI-assisted nucleated-cell assessment, the instrument preclassified a target of 200 white cells, after which a technician reviewed and corrected classifications.
The manual microscopy comparator used the same technician, the same smear A, and the same target cell count as the AI-assisted workflow.
The nucleated-cell reference standard used two senior morphology experts and third-reader adjudication when prespecified concordance criteria were not met.
A nucleated-cell result passed when the evaluated proportion fell within the expert reference result plus or minus 1.96 times the prespecified standard error.

outcome.definition: Evaluated result within reference result ±1.96 x SE

canonical_statement: Red-cell morphology was graded for 13 categories; schistocytes were graded 0, 1+, 2+, or 3+, while other morphologies were graded 0, 2+, or 3+.
For binary red-cell accuracy analyses, schistocytes graded at least 1+ and other red-cell morphologies graded at least 2+ were defined as positive.
The red-cell reference standard used independent blinded grades from two experts, with a third expert adjudicating disagreements using smear C.
For AI-assisted platelet estimation, the instrument identified platelets and red cells in scanned fields and combined the reviewed image counts with the LIS red-cell concentration.
Manual platelet estimation counted platelets in 10 oil-immersion fields and multiplied the average field count by 15.
The platelet reference method used repeated CD41/CD61 flow-cytometry measurements and the red-cell-to-platelet particle ratio to calculate platelet concentration.
The primary endpoints were nucleated-cell pass-rate superiority, red-cell morphology accuracy non-inferiority with a -5% margin, and agreement of platelet estimates with flow cytometry.

Total AI-assisted output time was defined as instrument processing plus technician review of white cells, red-cell grades, and platelet estimates; total control time was the sum of the three manual tasks.
APL screening was positive when abnormal promyelocytes exceeded 1%, using molecularly confirmed APL as the reference diagnosis.
Myelofibrosis screening was positive when teardrop cells were graded at least 2+, using the clinical diagnosis as the reference.
Superiority required the lower 95% confidence bound for the pooled risk difference to exceed zero, while red-cell non-inferiority used a prespecified -5% accuracy margin.
AI assistance increased the pooled lymphocyte pass rate by 10.79 percentage points relative to manual microscopy (95% CI 8.55 to 13.03).

canonical_statement: Low prevalence of several abnormal cell types and rare red-cell morphologies limited estimate precision and generalizability to uncommon hematologic diseases.
The study did not perform a comprehensive cell-level error analysis because no expert performed final validation of every instrument-derived classification.
All centers used the same smear-preparation equipment and standardized staining protocols, so external validation is needed across laboratories with different equipment and preprocessing conditions.
The evaluated system could not reliably identify malaria-infected red cells and could not assess smear-level red-cell arrangements such as rouleaux or agglutination.
The minimal dataset is not publicly available because it may contain identifying clinical information; deidentified data may be requested subject to institutional approval and a data-use agreement.
The authors reported that R scripts for preprocessing, statistical analysis, and figure generation were available in the supplementary file, with package versions documented.
Shenzhen Mindray Bio-Medical Electronics funded the regulatory clinical performance evaluation, supplied equipment, and coordinated multicenter activities.
The authors stated that the sponsor had no role in study design, conduct, analysis, interpretation, manuscript writing, or the publication decision.
Yi Ye and Jianping Xiao were employees of Shenzhen Mindray Bio-Medical Electronics; the other authors declared no competing interests.

The authors concluded that AI-assisted peripheral blood morphology improved efficiency and agreement with expert or flow-cytometry references and may function as structured decision support in routine hematology laboratories.
The study did not test whether AI-assisted morphology changed patient management or clinical outcomes, and the authors called for further prospective studies of those effects.
